newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Grieving Australia ski resort confronts its loss.
newsitem.headline: Grieving Australia ski resort confronts its loss.

text.p: Villagers of Thredbo, Australia's main winter playground, clung to each other in grief on Friday as hope turned to despair for family and friends of those entombed beneath a landslide.

About 100 people, traumatised and exhausted, gathered at Thredbo's sunlit chapel to pray for the 18 people still trapped in the rubble and to grieve for the two people whose lifeless bodies have been found.
The people of Thredbo, which has a permanent population of just a few hundred and is known for its cosy village atmosphere, turned to each other for comfort.
They have been told to expect the worst.

"We are like a family -- there's only about 300 people here," Father Wally Stefanski told reporters outside the chapel. "They are angry because their loved one is somewhere underground. They said they need some action."
Those missing have been buried since shortly before midnight on Wednesday and police said on Friday there was virtually no chance they would be found alive.

The landslide carried away two ski lodges in Thredbo, southwest of Sydney in Australia's Snowy Mountains, when a steep hillside gave way, sending one lodge into the other and burying all the occupants.
Most of the family and friends making their way into the chapel were distraught and exhausted. One woman, barely able to walk, sobbed uncontrollably as a relative guided her in.
But Stefanski said some families still believed there was a chance that survivors would be found.
"I pray for those, we don't know if they are alive or dead, but we still have hope," he said during the service.

More skiers returned to the slopes on Friday, but even those who made it on to the snow found it difficult to concentrate when they were confronted by the gash left by the landslide as they skied down the mountain.
"I tried to ski this morning, but I just lost it at about midday," one woman, a tourist from Canberra, told Reuters as she stared at the rubble. "I was just going all over the place."
The ruins of the lodges drew stares from around the village and even from the ski slopes where the laughter seemed to have gone out of a perfect cloudless sky.
Dour-looking ski instructors went through their paces with a few beginners who bothered to turn up for ski school, sending their pupils cheerlessly down a slope.
In the background, high on a facing slope, rescuers gingerly picked their way through the dirt, rocks and gum trees and concrete and twisted metal.
Relatives were not the only people feeling frustrated at the slow progress. Ambulance spokesman Graeme Field said paramedical staff felt particularly helpless.
"For the ambulance officers, your job is to help people. You know there's people there but can't do anything for them, so the feeling is mainly one of frustration," Field told Reuters.
About 30 people, most appearing to be relatives and friends of the trapped, kept a vigil on a hill opposite the wreckage.
They stood huddled in groups, talking quietly with arms around each other, watching for any sign of life.
